standard_text: Solve equations of the form x + p = q, x - p = q, px = q, and x/p = q fluently for cases in which p, q and x are all nonnegative rational numbers. Represent real-world problems using equations of these forms and solve such problems.

progression.narrative:
6.AF.3 demands two things, in a deliberate order: SOLVE one-step equations of the four forms x + p = q, x - p = q, px = q, and x/p = q fluently with nonnegative rationals, and REPRESENT real-world problems with those same equations and solve them. Solving comes first because it is one rhythm repeated four ways: name what is being done to x, undo it with the inverse operation on both sides, and check by substituting (S0). Representing is the harder half: a student has to decode a story's action into a form -- 'share equally' becomes division (S1), and 'two parts make a whole' becomes addition with the total standing alone on one side (S2).

On grade level, the two halves grow together. The solving mechanic matures to fraction and decimal coefficients, where 'divide both sides' becomes 'multiply by the reciprocal' (S3), and students learn what a solution IS -- the value that makes an equation true under substitution, not a number that happens to appear in it (S4). Then both halves run in sequence on real problems: translate 'N times as much' into px = q and solve (S5), and model a two-part decimal or fraction total as x + p = q, then solve with the inverse (S6) -- the spot where modeling (addition) and solving (subtraction) point in opposite directions. The ceiling of the standard is interpretation: a budget equation whose quotient is not whole, where the story -- not the rounding rule -- decides which way the answer moves (S7).

steps.rationale: The core mechanic on friendly whole numbers: name what is being done to x, undo it on both sides, check by substituting. Every later step of the standard reuses this exact rhythm.
The first act of the standard's 'represent real-world problems' demand: decode 'share equally' into a division equation (or its multiplication partner), with one action verb doing all the work.

Recognize part-part-whole structure: the total stands alone on one side while the parts -- including the unknown -- combine on the other. Choosing among near-miss equations sharpens what 'models the situation' means.
The solving mechanic goes on grade: coefficients become fractions and decimals, so 'divide both sides' matures into 'multiply by the reciprocal.' This is the fluency the standard names.

Own the meaning of 'solution': the value that makes an equation true under substitution -- never a number that merely appears in the equation. Substitution becomes the student's self-check for every other step.
Both halves together for multiplication: translate 'N times as much' into px = q, then solve. The known amount is the RESULT of the multiplying -- the structure students most often invert.

Both halves together for addition with grade-level numbers: model a two-part total as x + p = q, then solve with the inverse -- the spot where modeling (addition) and solving (subtraction) point in opposite directions.
The standard's ceiling: solve a decimal budget equation and make the answer make sense in context -- a non-whole quotient must be rounded the way the story demands, then defended in words.

skills.name: Use inverse operations to undo addition or multiplication

prerequisite_skill.description: Understand that addition and subtraction are opposites, and multiplication and division are opposites, so one undoes the other.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: If I add 7 to a number and get 12, what should I do to find the original number?

skills.i_do_script: Solving an equation means getting the variable alone on one side. To do that we use the OPPOSITE operation to undo what is happening to the variable. Watch: in x + 5 = 12, the x has 5 added to it, so I subtract 5 from BOTH sides and get x = 7. In 4x = 20, the x is multiplied by 4, so I divide BOTH sides by 4 and get x = 5. The rule is simple: addition undoes subtraction, multiplication undoes division.

canonical_error.pattern: Student uses the same operation that appears in the equation instead of its inverse.
canonical_error.example: For x + 5 = 12, student writes x = 12 + 5 = 17 instead of x = 12 - 5 = 7.
canonical_error.why: Student treats the equation as a string of symbols to compute left-to-right rather than a balance to undo. They have not internalized that solving means reversing what was done to x.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on. What is happening to x?
redirect_script.prompt: Point to x and say what is being done to it. If something is added, subtract on both sides. If something is multiplied, divide on both sides. The opposite undoes it.
redirect_script.praise: You picked the opposite operation. That's how solving works.

vocabulary.definition: The opposite operation that undoes another. Addition undoes subtraction; multiplication undoes division.
A math sentence that says two amounts are equal, with an equals sign in the middle.
A letter that stands in for a number we don't know yet.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to F2: Compute fluently with nonneg rationals.
next_steps.if_fail: Review opposite-operation fact families with whole numbers (3 + 4 = 7, 7 - 4 = 3) before returning.

sample_items.distractor_logic: Saying 'adding 6' repeats the visible operation -- the canonical undo error.
Saying 'subtracting 9' repeats the operation instead of reversing it.
Common slips: 'multiplying by 4' (repeat) or 'subtracting 4' (wrong inverse pair).
Common slips: 'dividing by 5' (repeat) or 'adding 5' (wrong inverse pair).

sample_items.stem: x + 8 = 15. What do you do to both sides?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 'Add 8' repeats the visible operation; 'subtract 15' targets the wrong number.

sample_items.stem: x - 3 = 10. What do you do to both sides?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 'Subtract 3' repeats the visible operation; 'add 10' targets the wrong number.

sample_items.stem: 6x = 30. What do you do to both sides?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 'Multiply by 6' repeats the operation; 'subtract 6' picks the wrong inverse pair.

sample_items.stem: x/4 = 3. What do you do to both sides?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 'Divide by 4' repeats the operation; 'add 4' picks the wrong inverse pair.

sample_items.stem: 5 + x = 11. What do you do to both sides?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 'Add 5' repeats the operation; 'subtract 11' targets the total instead of the added part.

sample_items.stem: 9x = 27. What do you do to both sides?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 'Multiply by 9' repeats the operation; 'divide by 27' flips which number is attached to x.

sample_items.stem: x - 12 = 4. What do you do to both sides?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 'Subtract 12' repeats the operation; 'subtract 4' operates on the result instead.

sample_items.stem: x/2 = 9. What do you do to both sides?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 'Divide by 2' repeats the operation; 'multiply by 9' targets the wrong number.

skills.name: Compute fluently with nonnegative fractions and decimals

prerequisite_skill.description: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide nonneg fractions, mixed numbers, and decimals without a calculator.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: What is 2.5 - 1.25? What is 3 1/3 divided by 2/3?

skills.i_do_script: On 6.AF.3 the calculator is not allowed, and many problems use decimals or fractions. Watch: 2.5 - 1.25. I line up the decimal points and subtract: 2.50 - 1.25 = 1.25. For fractions: 3 1/3 divided by 2/3 means 10/3 times 3/2 = 30/6 = 5. We need to be quick with these because solving the equation comes AFTER the arithmetic.

canonical_error.pattern: Student loses track of decimal place value or flips a fraction operation, producing arithmetic errors that hide a correct solving method.
canonical_error.example: For x + 1.25 = 2.5, student computes 2.5 - 1.25 = 1.35 (forgetting to align decimals) and reports x = 1.35 instead of 1.25.
canonical_error.why: Student has not automated rational-number arithmetic, so attention goes to the calculation and the equation-solving step suffers. Procedure for fractions vs decimals is not yet fluent.

redirect_script.stop: Pause — let's check the arithmetic only.
redirect_script.prompt: Set the equation aside and just do the subtraction (or division). Line up decimals point-under-point, or rewrite mixed numbers as improper fractions. Get the number first, then plug it back in.
redirect_script.praise: Clean arithmetic. Now the equation answer falls right out.

vocabulary.definition: Any number that can be written as a fraction, including whole numbers, decimals, and mixed numbers.
A whole number plus a fraction, like 3 1/3.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to S1 (Looking Back) or directly to on-grade skills if Looking Back is also solid.
next_steps.if_fail: Review fraction/decimal arithmetic procedures using a number line or grid model.

sample_items.distractor_logic: 1.35 comes from misaligned decimal places (subtracting 2.5 - 1.2 and appending 5).
0.80 comes from adding 5 to the hundredths place instead of 5 tenths.
20 comes from ignoring the decimal point; 4.5 comes from adding instead.
3 comes from halving instead of asking 'how many halves fit in 6.'
2/6 comes from adding numerators and denominators straight across.
2/2 comes from subtracting straight across; needs the common denominator 2/4.
16 comes from dividing by 1/2 instead of taking half; 8 1/2 comes from adding.
1 1/2 comes from multiplying by 1/2 instead of asking 'how many halves in 3.'
18 comes from dividing by 2/3; 24/3 left unsimplified is fine to accept as 8.
4.5 comes from subtracting only the whole-number part.
60 comes from dropping the decimal point; 6.2 from adding instead.
4 1/4 comes from subtracting the fraction parts without regrouping (1/2 - 3/4 flipped).

skills.name: Solve a one-step whole-number equation

prerequisite_skill.description: Use a known fact family (addition/subtraction or multiplication/division) to find an unknown whole number in a number sentence.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: What number goes in the box to make the equation true: 8 + [] = 15?

skills.i_do_script: When I see an equation like x + 5 = 12, I want to get x by itself. I ask: what is being done to x? Here, 5 is being added to x. To undo addition, I subtract 5 from BOTH sides. That gives me x = 12 - 5, so x = 7. I check by substituting: 7 + 5 = 12. It works. The same idea works for every form: subtraction is undone by addition, multiplication is undone by division, and division is undone by multiplication. Always do the same thing to both sides and always check by plugging the answer back in.

canonical_error.pattern: Student performs the same operation that already appears in the equation instead of its inverse, especially confusing 'undo' with 'repeat.'
canonical_error.example: For x + 7 = 15, student writes x = 15 + 7 = 22 instead of x = 15 - 7 = 8.
canonical_error.why: Student treats the visible operation as the instruction ('I see plus, so I add') rather than asking what action would isolate x. They have not yet built the substitute-and-check habit that would catch the mistake.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- before you solve, ask: what is happening to x in this equation?
redirect_script.prompt: Name the operation you see attached to x, then name its OPPOSITE. Plus and minus are opposites. Times and divide are opposites. Do the opposite to BOTH sides, then plug your answer back in to check.
redirect_script.praise: You named the inverse operation, applied it to both sides, and checked by substituting. That is exactly the rhythm that makes every one-step equation feel the same.

vocabulary.definition: A math sentence that says two expressions are equal, with an equals sign between them. Example: x + 4 = 9.
A letter that stands for an unknown number. In x + 4 = 9, the variable is x.
The operation that undoes another. Addition and subtraction are inverses; multiplication and division are inverses.
The value of the variable that makes the equation true. You can verify a solution by substituting it back into the original equation.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to S3: Solve a one-step multiplication equation px = q for x using grade-level rational coefficients.
next_steps.if_fail: Return to F1 and practice naming the inverse operation pair before attempting any equation.
